reviewedContributions.name: Personal & Professional Development

evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
evidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

reviewedContributions.finding: Required first-year academic and personal development; not a target-generated elective.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Economics

evidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
evidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
evidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
evidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

reviewedContributions.finding: Scarcity, incentives, consumer choice and market behaviour provide an economic foundation for resource-allocation and policy questions; no health-economic evaluation technique is inferred.

reviewedContributions.name: Public Economics

evidence.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
evidence.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
evidence.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
evidence.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

reviewedContributions.finding: Public goods, externalities, efficiency/equity, health and welfare expenditure, insurance and redistribution directly support health-policy allocation questions; not a dedicated cost-effectiveness course.

reviewedContributions.name: Econometrics

evidence.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

reviewedContributions.finding: OLS, GLS, instrumental variables, inference, causal/predictive economic modelling and an empirical paper support evaluating social-policy evidence; given full weight from the official description.

reviewedContributions.name: Research Methods & Statistics

evidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
evidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
evidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
evidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Research questions, measurement, surveys, experiments, inferential statistics and an ethical empirical project directly supply social/behavioural research foundations.

reviewedContributions.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure

evidence.description2: What does it take to lead effectively through pressure, conflict, and diversity? Explore how emotion, identity, belonging, and inclusion shape leadership, teamwork, and performance. Design and conduct an original empirical study while building career-ready skills in research design, data analysis, teamwork, ethical decision-making, and scientific communication.
evidence.profile: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, emotional expression and suppression, emotional labor, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership and social interaction under conflict, exclusion and interpersonal uncertainty. It emphasises inclusive leadership and ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences, with digital emotion regulation as a further strand. Students conduct a supervised quantitative survey project: formulating theory-driven hypotheses, selecting established psychological measures, designing and piloting a Qualtrics survey, recruiting participants ethically, collecting original data and preparing a clean dataset. Individual work applies descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio, and interprets findings and limitations in empirical reports and evidence-based leadership recommendations.
evidence.topics: Emotion regulation strategies; Emotional intelligence; Emotional expression and suppression; Emotional labor; Inclusive leadership; Belonging and identity safety; Psychological safety; Ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences; Digital emotion regulation; Psychological measurement, reliability and validity; Ethical survey research in diverse populations; Interpretation and limitations of quantitative evidence; Evidence-based leadership recommendations
evidence.methods: Theory-driven hypothesis formulation; Quantitative survey research; Established psychological measure selection and evaluation; Qualtrics survey construction and piloting; Ethical participant recruitment and original data collection; Codebook development, reverse coding and scale scoring; Data cleaning and missing-data documentation; Descriptive statistics; Reliability analysis; Correlation analysis; Group comparisons; Introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio; APA-style empirical reporting

reviewedContributions.finding: Belonging, identity safety, inclusion, emotional regulation and an original survey project support wellbeing and unequal social environments and develop empirical behavioural evidence.

reviewedContributions.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership

evidence.description2: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
evidence.profile: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
evidence.topics: Diversity, equity and inclusion; Job attitudes and satisfaction; Emotions, stress and workplace health; Personality and individual differences; Perception and decision-making; Motivation; Group behaviour and work teams; Human resource systems; Communication, conflict and negotiation; Leadership, power and politics; Organizational structure; Organizational culture and change
evidence.methods: Organizational case analysis; Research design and hypothesis formulation; Systematic literature review; PRISMA flow diagrams and checklists; Database searching and study screening; Source-quality appraisal and evidence synthesis

reviewedContributions.finding: Organisational structure, culture, teams, change and workplace health, with systematic-review practice, support understanding health organisations; patient-centred healthcare innovation remains a different specialism.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Data Science

evidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
evidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
evidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
evidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: R cleaning, manipulation, visualisation and spatial/text data analysis support empirical health and social research; this complements rather than replaces inferential statistics.

reviewedContributions.name: Governance of Sustainability

evidence.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
evidence.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
evidence.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
evidence.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

reviewedContributions.finding: Institutions, actors, participation, public goods and policy advice/evaluation on food, water, energy and climate support collective decisions about healthy environments; no direct urban-health fieldwork equivalence.

reviewedContributions.name: Climate Change

evidence.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
evidence.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
evidence.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
evidence.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

reviewedContributions.finding: Climate impacts including health, climate justice, adaptation and stakeholder communication provide a substantive environmental-health context; not a neighbourhood health-design course.

reviewedContributions.name: Calling Bullshit

evidence.description2: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.
evidence.profile: Examines misinformation through philosophy, history, psychology and practical information evaluation. Students distinguish misleading discourse from related concepts, investigate cognitive and social vulnerabilities, and analyze pseudoscience, statistical misrepresentation and reasoning errors. Fact-checking, deepfake production and response exercises develop recognition and intervention skills. Projects map a misinformation narrative's actors and circulation and produce a research-grounded myth-debunking video with an external interview.
evidence.topics: Bullshit, lying and misinformation; Historical hoaxes and propaganda; Cognitive bias and motivated reasoning; Social identity and information overload; Scientific credibility and pseudoscience; Publication bias and misconduct; Misleading statistics and data displays; Reasoning fallacies; Deepfakes; Misinformation diffusion; Debunking and counter-narratives; Medical and climate misinformation
evidence.methods: Source-credibility evaluation; Fact-checking protocols; Reasoning-fallacy detection; Critical analysis of statistical claims; Misinformation-network mapping; Deepfake video construction and analysis; Debunking-message design; Expert interviewing; Documentary-style explanatory video production

reviewedContributions.finding: Medical and climate misinformation, scientific credibility, diffusion and research-grounded debunking messages directly support critical public-health communication and trust.

reviewedContributions.name: Law, Society & Justice

evidence.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
evidence.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
evidence.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
evidence.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review

reviewedContributions.finding: Rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender in law supply legal/normative tools for analysing unequal institutions; no specific health regulation is claimed.

reviewedContributions.name: Ethics

evidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
evidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
evidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
evidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

reviewedContributions.finding: Moral argument, care ethics, autonomy and justice-related reasoning provide substantive ethical tools for contested health decisions, without claiming a specialist health-law curriculum.

reviewedContributions.name: Philosophy of Emotion

evidence.description2: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.
evidence.profile: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
evidence.topics: Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories of emotion; Ancient Greek and Indian accounts of emotion; Epistemic emotions; Emotion and decision-making; Love; Fear and existential anxiety; Mood and grief; Moral emotions; Gender and emotion; Political love and anger; Racial injustice; Temporality of emotion; Emotion and artistic expression
evidence.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual and argumentative analysis; Phenomenological description of emotional experience; Critical comparison of emotion theories

reviewedContributions.finding: Philosophical emotion analysis is academically defensible background but less central than structured inequality/institutions and health/behaviour evidence in the completed programmes.

reviewedContributions.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics

evidence.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
evidence.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
evidence.topics: Democracy and authoritarianism; Democratization and democratic backsliding; States, nations and nationalism; Constitutions and courts; Executives, legislatures and bureaucracies; Political economy; Parties and party systems; Populism and technocracy; Elections and electoral systems; Political culture and polarization; Political participation; Interest groups and public policy
evidence.methods: Theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; Concept operationalization and democracy measurement; V-Dem data analysis; Comparative case analysis; Academic literature searching with OpenAlex and AI tools; Empirical election analysis; Research-question formulation

reviewedContributions.finding: Political institutions, representation, interests and empirical comparative analysis provide the political framework in which collective health-policy choices occur.

reviewedContributions.name: European Union Politics

evidence.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
evidence.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
evidence.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
evidence.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: EU institutions, interests, legislation and implementation supply a specific supranational level of health-relevant governance; health policy is an application, not the entire course.

reviewedContributions.name: Public Policy Analysis

evidence.description2: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.

reviewedContributions.finding: The official description supports policy-making phases across national/international arenas, a sugar case and policy-memo writing. These directly support policy analysis; no unlisted health-policy theory or method is inferred.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Sociology

evidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
evidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
evidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
evidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

reviewedContributions.finding: Social structure, stratification, class, race, gender and inequality provide substantive sociological tools for analysing social determinants of health; applications are broader than health sociology.

reviewedContributions.name: Qualitative Research Methodology

evidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
evidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
evidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
evidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

reviewedContributions.finding: Interviews, focus groups, ethics, reflexivity, coding and a qualitative research project directly support inquiry into lived health, community practices and unequal environments.

reviewedContributions.name: Modern Sociology

evidence.description2: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
evidence.profile: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
evidence.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power
evidence.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research

reviewedContributions.finding: Intersectionality, stigma, othering, social space, gender and colonial power deepen the theoretical analysis of structural health inequality; not a specialist public-health course.

reviewedContributions.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice

evidence.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

reviewedContributions.finding: Description-supported movement theory and environmental justice, including feminist and anti-colonial perspectives, directly deepen collective-action and unequal-environment analysis; absent outline detail is not invented.

reviewedContributions.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

evidence.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
evidence.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
evidence.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
evidence.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design

reviewedContributions.finding: Civil society, trust, solidarity, public spheres and empirical study of civic organisations supply specific methods and theory for community participation and collective health action.

reviewedContributions.name: Epidemiology & Public Health

evidence.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
evidence.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
evidence.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
evidence.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development

reviewedContributions.finding: Direct epidemiology, disease measures, bias and causality, social/environmental determinants and a local population-health intervention project supply the public-health core.

reviewedContributions.name: Infection & Immunity

evidence.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
evidence.profile: Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.
evidence.topics: Infectious agents and microbial virulence; Host defence and immune evasion; Immune cells, organs and cytokines; Innate immunity and complement; Antibodies and antigen recognition; MHC and lymphocyte receptors; Lymphocyte activation, development and memory; Cell- and antibody-mediated immunity; Mucosal immunity; Vaccination and viral infections; Hypersensitivity and allergy; Immunodeficiency; Autoimmune disease; Outbreak management
evidence.methods: Flow-cytometry data analysis and lymphocyte phenotyping; Clinical symptom and mechanism analysis; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Critical analysis of immunological research; Graphical synthesis of scientific findings

reviewedContributions.finding: Immunological mechanisms, flow cytometry, clinical cases and research appraisal were considered. Vaccination/outbreak relevance does not make this a social prevention or programme-level substitute; stronger social-health content selected.

reviewedContributions.name: Mechanisms of Disease

evidence.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.
evidence.profile: Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.
evidence.topics: Organ-system disease mechanisms; Nutrition and digestive disease; Hematological and cardiovascular disease; Respiratory disease; Renal failure, dialysis and transplantation; Endocrine disorders; Neurological disease; Etiology and pathogenesis; Diagnosis, treatment and prognosis; Medical ethics; Rheumatic disease
evidence.methods: Clinical case analysis; Differential diagnosis reasoning; Critical appraisal of diagnostic and laboratory procedures; Integration of anatomy, physiology and clinical evidence; Mechanistic modelling of an imaginary disease; Biomedical literature comparison

reviewedContributions.finding: Pathophysiology, diagnosis/treatment and mechanistic cases are not the multilevel preventive-intervention framework; false alignment removed and course weight redirected to defining social-health content.

reviewedContributions.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine

evidence.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
evidence.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
evidence.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
evidence.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments

reviewedContributions.finding: Considered molecular/cellular foundations fully; not needed as a gateway once clinical/biomedical electives are withdrawn. Their programme weight displaced defining social/preventive-health substance.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior

evidence.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
evidence.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
evidence.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
evidence.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Psychological and neural explanations of learning, social influence and mental processes provide the gateway to health and behavioural psychology; not an introduction to population-health systems.

reviewedContributions.name: Human Physiology

evidence.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
evidence.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
evidence.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
evidence.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision

reviewedContributions.finding: Normal organ physiology is real substantive preparation for biomedical study, but is a weaker defining choice here than the target’s social determinants, policy, behaviour and methods; removed rather than calling it unavailable academically.

reviewedContributions.name: Social Psychology

evidence.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
evidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
evidence.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
evidence.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study

reviewedContributions.finding: Social influence, attitudes, persuasion, prejudice and group behaviour directly support understanding health choices and social intervention; the research-design task develops evidence appraisal.

reviewedContributions.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods

evidence.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
evidence.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
evidence.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
evidence.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting

reviewedContributions.finding: Research design, regression, group comparisons, logistic models, reliability and R analysis support evaluating health and behavioural evidence; no claim of full epidemiological or qualitative-methods coverage.

reviewedContributions.name: Psychopathology

evidence.description2: The Psychopathology course offers a deep dive into the factors shaping mental health across the lifespan. Students will develop critical thinking skills, explore the bio-psycho-social approach, and gain a comprehensive understanding of mental health and its disorders. Through key concepts, research findings, and psychological assessment techniques, this course empowers individuals to promote wellness and make a meaningful impact in both personal and professional spheres.
evidence.profile: Examines mental health and psychopathology across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial perspective. Historical views, classification and assessment frame biological, psychological, cultural and social explanations of disorders and treatment. Case-based work applies diagnostic concepts to varied presentations. A structured literature-based essay investigates a focused mental-health question through explicit searching, source selection, evidence appraisal and synthesis, with optional use of PRISMA reporting tools.
evidence.topics: Mental-disorder concepts and stigma; Historical and contemporary psychopathology; Biopsychosocial causation; Clinical assessment and diagnostic classification; Stress and health; Anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders; Mood disorders; Somatic and dissociative disorders; Psychotic disorders; Eating and personality disorders; Substance-related and neurocognitive disorders; Sexuality and mental health; Childhood and adolescent disorders; Forensic psychology; Culture and emotion regulation
evidence.methods: Diagnostic case analysis; Application and critique of DSM criteria; Biopsychosocial case formulation; Structured literature searching and screening; Source-quality appraisal; Evidence synthesis; Critical evaluation of etiological and intervention models

reviewedContributions.finding: Biopsychosocial psychopathology and literature appraisal are relevant mental-health complements, but a disorders-focused course was displaced by methods, policy or developmental/community prevention according to each programme’s priorities.

reviewedContributions.name: Medical & Health Psychology

evidence.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
evidence.profile: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
evidence.topics: Biopsychosocial model; Health inequalities; Health-risk and protective behaviours; Behaviour-change models; Prevention; Stress and coping; Symptom perception; Somatic symptom disorders; Medical consultation; Shared decision-making; Doctor–patient communication; Pain; Chronic illness; Family and caregiver experiences; Quality of life; Cultural competence; Support for healthcare professionals
evidence.methods: Psychological case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of health-psychology research and interventions; Clinical-health case formulation; Interviewing-skills practice; Cultural Formulation Interview analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Biopsychosocial health, inequalities, health behaviours, prevention, stress, coping and patient communication directly implement health psychology; clinical settings are one part of its content.

reviewedContributions.name: Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies

evidence.description2: Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.
evidence.profile: Introduces clinical psychological assessment and major psychotherapeutic approaches across the lifespan. Students study ethics, diagnostic systems, test reliability and validity, interviews, personality and cognitive assessment, then psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, systemic and integrative treatments. Training sessions develop introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A psychodiagnostic case report integrates findings and treatment recommendations, while self-monitoring examines developing clinical skills.
evidence.topics: Clinical attitude and ethics; Diagnostic classification; Reliability and validity; Clinical interviews; Personality inventories and projective techniques; Cognitive and neuropsychological assessment; Behavioural and biological assessment; Psychological reporting; Psychodynamic and behavioural therapies; Cognitive therapy and CBT; Person-centered and family therapies; Integrative psychotherapy; Treatment outcomes and evidence; Child and adolescent clinical psychology
evidence.methods: Clinical interviewing practice; Introductory psychological-test administration, scoring and interpretation; Psychometric appraisal; Behavioural observation; Integration of assessment data; Psychodiagnostic report writing; Clinical case and therapy-session analysis; Reflective monitoring of clinical skills

reviewedContributions.finding: Assessment and psychotherapeutic approaches are real clinical training, not social-health policy or population prevention. Removed clinical emphasis; no licence-based no-match inferred.

reviewedContributions.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics

evidence.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
evidence.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
evidence.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
evidence.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting

reviewedContributions.finding: Systematic review, study selection, risk of bias, effect sizes and R meta-analysis directly support critical synthesis of health/behavioural intervention evidence.

reviewedContributions.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology

evidence.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
evidence.profile: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
evidence.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
evidence.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports

reviewedContributions.finding: Development across the lifespan, environmental influences, care and a life-story interview support age-sensitive understanding of health and behaviour. Individual development is not health demography.

reviewedContributions.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism

evidence.description2: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
evidence.profile: Examines youth radicalization and educational prevention through psychology, education, sociology, political science and peace education. Models of radicalization and adolescent risk and protective factors lead into inclusive school climates, belonging, social-emotional learning, dialogue, media literacy and civic agency. Students translate primary research into teacher-training materials and a youth toolkit for an international school project, then revise the resources using feedback from intended recipients.
evidence.topics: Radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism; Developmental and psychosocial pathways; Risk and protective factors; School climate and belonging; Identity and peer influence; Social-emotional learning and well-being; Empathy and perspective-taking; Conflict resolution and intercultural dialogue; Mental-health literacy and referral; Digital literacy and misinformation; Youth leadership and democratic participation; Counter- and alternative narratives
evidence.methods: Primary-research synthesis; Intervention-evidence appraisal; Case and classroom-scenario analysis; Inclusive educational-resource design; Alternative-narrative development; Recipient-feedback collection and iterative revision; Ethical appraisal of prevention tools

reviewedContributions.finding: Research-based youth prevention, mental wellbeing, school inclusion, media literacy and feedback-revised educational tools support evidence-informed community intervention. Radicalisation is a specific application, not the health programme’s defining topic.

reviewedContributions.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication

evidence.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
evidence.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
evidence.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
evidence.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

reviewedContributions.finding: Rhetorical argument, persuasion, speeches and audience-directed educational storytelling provide communication practice supporting public explanation and behaviour-change messages.

reviewedContributions.name: Style & Meaning

evidence.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
evidence.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
evidence.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
evidence.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

reviewedContributions.finding: Linguistic stylistics and literary interpretation were considered, but the supported behaviour/communication direction is stronger with practical persuasion, misinformation and inclusive audience work.

reviewedContributions.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis

evidence.description2: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

reviewedContributions.finding: Description-supported analysis of contested climate communication across texts, films and social media, culminating in participation in public debate, complements public-health/environmental communication questions.

reviewedContributions.name: Rhetoric in Action

evidence.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
evidence.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
evidence.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
evidence.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation

reviewedContributions.finding: Community work with children designs and revises age-appropriate rhetorical teaching activities. This specifically complements audience-sensitive intervention communication, not clinical or health-intervention expertise.

reviewedContributions.name: Persuasive Communication

evidence.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
evidence.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
evidence.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
evidence.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

reviewedContributions.finding: Ethical persuasion, framing, cognitive shortcuts and applied community messaging on sustainable lifestyles provide a specific behaviour-change communication contribution. Health intervention mapping is not reproduced.

reviewedContributions.name: Creative Communication Laboratory

evidence.description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.
evidence.profile: Studies and develops creative communication through poetry, performance and critically articulated artistic practice. Students move from lyric foundations to constrained and experimental forms, attending to sound, rhythm, imagery, voice and embodiment. Close reading and creative workshops lead into an independent traditional or hybrid project grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require students to justify formal, conceptual and procedural choices.
evidence.topics: Meaning and formal experimentation; Lyric poetry; Poetic sound and rhythm; Imagery and voice; Embodiment and performance; Constraint and formal deviation; Experimental poetry; Hybrid and digitally mediated forms; Creative process and revision; Aesthetic traditions and conceptual coherence
evidence.methods: Close poetic reading and listening; Constraint-based composition; Poetic and performative experimentation; Structured drafting and revision; Critical analysis of creative decisions; Independent practice-based creative inquiry

reviewedContributions.finding: Poetic/performance practice is substantive creative study, but not a strong health-behaviour implementation priority. Replaced with research-based communication/intervention evidence.

reviewedContributions.name: Media Archaeology

evidence.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
evidence.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
evidence.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
evidence.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research

reviewedContributions.finding: Material/historical media archaeology is fully considered; contemporary mediated attitudes, disability representation and documentary evidence more directly support this target’s communication priority.

reviewedContributions.name: From T.V. to TikTok

evidence.description2: Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.
evidence.profile: Examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Storytelling, power and representation connect television, film and digital forms to conformity, identity and imagined futures. Students analyze 1950s media, compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, and investigate disability representation. Futures-oriented projects create a speculative television-episode proposal and imagine possibilities that center disabled people.
evidence.topics: Media storytelling and power; American everyday life; 1950s television and conformity; Science fiction and social anxieties; Media futures and marginalization; Indigenous representation and self-representation; Disability stereotypes and visibility; Authentic voice and cultural agency; Future foresight and inclusive scenarios
evidence.methods: Historical analysis of primary media sources; Comparative representation analysis; Future-foresight scenario development; Theory-based speculative narrative design; Disability-centered futures inquiry

reviewedContributions.finding: Disability representation, media stereotypes, authentic voice and inclusive futures provide substantive critical analysis of how mediated messages shape attitudes toward wellbeing and marginalised groups.

reviewedContributions.name: Media & Race

evidence.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
evidence.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
evidence.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
evidence.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

reviewedContributions.finding: Systemic racial construction, exclusion, marginalized voices and participatory/archival media inquiry supply a sustained social-inequality and representation contribution; not a claim of health-specific communication training.

reviewedContributions.name: The Documentary

evidence.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
evidence.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
evidence.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
evidence.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice

reviewedContributions.finding: Documentary research, interviewing, representation ethics and producing a short film supply complementary practical tools for communicating social/health evidence; no compulsory health film is assumed.

programmeChecks.label: Population health, behaviour and social policy
Health inequalities, institutions and public policy
Health behaviour, evidence and public communication

alignmentRows: Both teach disease measures, epidemiological study designs, bias and public-health evidence. The programmes differ in applications and scope.
Both directly teach social influence, attitudes, group behaviour and the social-psychological study of behaviour.
Both directly study health behaviour, stress and coping, mental health and biopsychosocial evidence. UCR also emphasises patients and medical settings; WUR includes a quantitative group study.

The UCR programme combines public health and social sciences across several courses. No single selected course integrates the WUR introduction’s health systems, history, prevention and societal determinants.
No selected course provides the full global-health and health-promotion framework, international priority setting and health-system collaboration.
Social and health psychology contribute to behaviour, but no selected course sustains the specific biological, psychological and socioeconomic study of nutrition behaviour.
Climate and governance courses support environmental-health interests but do not reproduce the integrated neighbourhood health field-research and healthy-design assignment.
Public health, health psychology and communication contribute to prevention, but no single separately placed course integrates the WUR multilevel infectious/chronic disease-prevention framework.
Lifespan psychology studies individual development; it does not supply population demographic measures, transitions and quantitative health-demography research.

Public goods, equity, redistribution, health expenditure and social insurance directly address public allocation for a healthy society. WUR additionally teaches dedicated health-economic evaluation and wider economic perspectives.
Organisational culture, collaboration, leadership and change address an important organisational part of healthcare innovation. WUR’s patient-centred and frugal innovation design is not reproduced.

Misinformation, scientific trust, cognitive/social vulnerabilities and health/climate communication address an important part of the WUR course. WUR additionally teaches agenda setting, media and political communication across countries.

Ethical theory and critical moral argument supply a central part of reasoning about health, justice and autonomy. WUR concentrates on health-policy dilemmas; UCR has broader philosophical applications.

Policy-making phases, national/international arenas, a sugar-policy case and policy memos directly address policy analysis. WUR focuses more fully on health systems, participatory health promotion and policy networks.
Both teach sociological theory, social structure and inequality. WUR applies these throughout to health; UCR develops broader social cases.
Speech preparation and delivery, persuasive appeals and feedback-based communication practice address the specific presentation-skills function. UCR is a larger rhetoric course.

Theory-based persuasive messages, implementation with community partners and reflective evaluation address the communication part of behaviour-change intervention. WUR additionally requires systematic health Intervention Mapping and broader determinant/implementation planning.
No selected course provides the dedicated historical study of demographic, epidemiological, nutritional and welfare-state transitions.
No selected course sustains the specific sociological study of eating customs, food identity, access and health across cultural settings.
Both develop research questions and social-science research design, including experimental and nonexperimental approaches. The UCR course adds statistical analysis and an empirical project.

Regression, group comparisons, categorical outcomes and R-based research analysis share substantial quantitative methods. WUR also integrates qualitative analysis, mixed methods and survival analysis.
Both teach systematic literature searching, selection and critical evidence appraisal. UCR additionally develops quantitative meta-analysis; WUR also teaches scoping reviews.

Foundational statistical content occurs within broader selected methods courses, which are placed against their strongest research-design and data-analysis relationships; no separate course is duplicated here.
Inference and regression occur in the selected methods sequence. Those courses are placed against research design and data analysis rather than duplicated as a separate statistics course.
The required 18-credit WUR thesis differs from scheduled UCR courses. Optional UCR independent research is shown separately, outside each 180-credit programme.
This is genuine open elective space, without an invented course counterpart.
findings: Concepts tested before schedules: closest integrates epidemiology,healthpsychology,inequality,publiceconomics/policy,mixedresearch andenvironmentalgovernance. It materially responds to the target’s social-health core, not a biomedical substitute with incidental social electives. The second changes priority through law,redistribution,EU institutions,environmentaljustice,econometricpolicy evidence andracialrepresentation. The third sustains health/behaviour evidence,communication,persuasion,misinformation andaudience/communitywork. Healthpsychology andepidemiology anchor thetarget contribution; climate/documentary/school/extremism settings arebounded complementarymethods,not relabelledclinicalhealthcourses.
